Poise

POYZ -- from Old French pois, 'weight,' from Latin pendere, 'to weigh, to hang': a mind perfectly balanced. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Poise is grace, elegance, and dignity, especially under pressure.

Even at fourteen, the skater carried herself with the poise of a seasoned performer.

Worked Example

A speaker's microphone dies halfway through her talk; she waits a beat, smiles at the audience, raises her voice, and finishes as though nothing had happened.

Calm dignity that holds up when something goes wrong is exactly what poise means. Unlike 'confidence,' which is a feeling inside a person, poise is how that steadiness looks from the outside.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

composure: calm control of yourself

elegance: graceful, polished style

dignity: a bearing that commands respect

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

panic: sudden uncontrollable fear

awkwardness: clumsy discomfort in front of others

Where it sits · how much outward polish joins the calm — composure → poise → elegance

composure vs. poise: Composure is the plain core of poise -- staying calm inside -- while poise adds an outward grace and dignity to that calm.

elegance vs. poise: Elegance is showier than poise: poise is calm dignity that holds up when things go wrong, while elegance is polished beauty of style, whether or not anything is at stake.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — poise

root — poise: weight; to weigh (Old French (pois), from Latin pensum / pendere ('to weigh, to hang'))

Put it together

Put it together: Old French pois meant 'weight,' from Latin pendere, 'to weigh or hang.' Poise first named perfect balance -- a scale hanging level -- and English carried that image over to people: someone with poise is perfectly balanced under pressure. The same root gives us suspend and pendulum.

Use the root in a new word: suspend

Use the root in a new word: suspend: Workers suspend the chandelier from three heavy iron chains.

This unit teaches poise as calm, graceful self-control -- 'she handled the crisis with poise.' Poise is also a verb meaning to hold something balanced and ready ('poised to strike'), but that physical sense is not the one tested here.
